plot_extraction.response_text:
John Adderley Syson, now married and living away from his childhood home, returns to the countryside and farm where he once courted Hilda Millership. On his way, he meets Arthur Pilbeam, a young gamekeeper who is now Hilda’s lover and resents Syson’s continued letters and gifts to her.

At the farm, Syson and Hilda revisit their shared past, but he gradually realizes that he had idealized her and never understood her true nature. Hilda explains that she has found freedom and fulfillment in her relationship with Arthur, whom she loves on her own terms. She also accuses Syson of trying to shape her into someone she was not, while he counters that she encouraged the ambitions that drew him away from her.

After an uneasy meeting among all three, Syson leaves wounded by the recognition that his imagined spiritual bond with Hilda never truly existed. Secretly observing Hilda comforting and embracing Arthur, he hears her affirm that Syson has passed entirely out of her life, though she resists marrying Arthur immediately because she values the beauty and independence of their present relationship. Accepting the final separation between himself and Hilda, Syson returns to town.

style_extraction.response_text:
The story uses a psychologically intense, early modernist realism in which external landscape and inward emotion continually reflect, disturb, and reinterpret one another. Its third-person narration remains closely aligned with Syson for most of the story, moving freely between observable action, subjective perception, memory, and direct thought. The perspective is intimate but not wholly sympathetic: Syson’s sensitivity, vanity, nostalgia, self-contempt, and habit of idealising others are all exposed. At significant moments the narration also enters Hilda’s consciousness, revealing motives and insights unavailable to him. This subtle mobility of viewpoint turns the encounter into a contest between incompatible inner realities rather than a simple romantic confrontation.

The prose is richly sensory and strongly visual, especially in its treatment of the countryside. Colour is unusually prominent: bluebells become “azure shallows,” primroses appear in scarlet, pink, and pale purple, pine trunks are brick-red and purplish, and marigolds cast gold onto brown water. Landscape is rarely neutral description. It is animated through metaphor and personification: hazel branches spread “glad little hands,” daffodils resemble “yellow, ruffled birds,” hills wear woods like bearskin garments, and birdsong seems to condense from sunshine. Such images often fuse precise natural observation with lyrical transformation. Botanical and ornithological specificity—woodruff, dog-mercury, hyacinth, milkwort, lousewort, linnets, buntings, kingfishers—gives the setting material authority, while figurative language makes it visionary and emotionally charged.

A central stylistic tension exists between permanence and change. Repetition of phrases such as “still,” “unaltered,” and “back” initially presents the landscape as an “eternal” world preserved from Syson’s youth. Yet the apparent continuity of place throws human change into sharper relief. The familiar countryside survives, but the emotional meaning Syson once assigned to it collapses. Natural beauty therefore produces both exaltation and pain. Even at the end, when the world remains “marvellous, for ever new,” Syson experiences it as a kind of “monotone hell.” This characteristic doubleness allows beauty and anguish to occupy the same image.

The diction moves between lyrical refinement, philosophical abstraction, plain rural speech, and occasional literary allusion. The narrator’s vocabulary is often elevated and exact, using words such as “diapered,” “sublimation,” “phosphorescence,” and “truncheon,” while local characters speak in contracted dialect forms such as “lodgin’,” “goin’,” “allus,” “a’ready,” and “ter.” Dialect is rendered lightly rather than phonetically throughout, enough to establish regional and class difference without making the dialogue difficult to read. Syson’s cultivated register, quotations, poetry books, French verse, and references to Dante, Botticelli, William Morris, and classical gods mark both his education and his tendency to filter experience through art. These allusions are not merely decorative: they expose his habit of turning Hilda into an imagined Beatrice, nun, angel, or poetic symbol instead of recognising her autonomous identity.

Sentence structure alternates between expansive descriptive passages and abrupt dramatic exchanges. Landscape sentences frequently accumulate clauses, colours, textures, and comparisons, creating a flowing, immersive rhythm. Emotional shocks are conveyed through short statements, fragments, exclamations, and sudden questions: “You?—Addy!”, “I’m married myself,” and “I was married the same night as you.” Dashes, semicolons, ellipses, and pauses reproduce hesitation, withheld feeling, and shifts in power. Repeated silences are especially important. Characters often fail to answer directly, and the narrative records pauses as active moments in which pride, jealousy, fear, and calculation operate beneath speech.

Dialogue is adversarial and oblique. Conversations proceed through challenges, evasions, ironic repetitions, and statements whose implications are more important than their literal content. The encounter with Pilbeam begins as a dispute over trespass but quickly becomes a struggle over sexual and social territory. Syson and Hilda similarly debate love through abstractions about freedom, selfhood, gods, soil, and personal development. Their speech often wounds indirectly. Irony functions as a defence, especially for Syson, whose “brilliant” laughter and cultivated wit repeatedly conceal humiliation. Hilda’s quieter, more assured speech gradually gains dominance, and her use of the shared language once created with Syson demonstrates that she has absorbed and appropriated what he believed belonged to their relationship.

Character description is physical, evaluative, and psychologically suggestive. Pilbeam’s thrusting chest and balanced body make him seem “taut with animal life,” while Hilda’s arms, throat, hair, and posture are described through images of plants, kernels, crowns, and fur. Bodies disclose forms of being: Pilbeam is instinctive and embodied; Hilda is rooted, self-contained, and increasingly sensual; Syson is mobile, analytical, luminous, and divided against himself. The story repeatedly opposes intellectual or aesthetic possession to bodily and local belonging. Hilda’s declaration that she is “like a plant” able to grow only in her own soil encapsulates this organic conception of identity.

The three-part structure traces a progressive dismantling of illusion. The first section restores Syson’s past through landscape, then disrupts it through his meeting with Pilbeam. The second brings him into Hilda’s domestic and natural world, where familiarity gives way to estrangement. The third reveals the keeper’s hut, Hilda’s sexual independence, and the final collapse of Syson’s idealised history. Spatial movement carries symbolic force: Syson passes from open views into increasingly enclosed and shadowed paths, reaches the secret inner room of the hut, and then returns toward open country with painful knowledge. Thresholds, gates, woodland paths, windows, and concealed compartments repeatedly mark transitions between memory and actuality, public identity and private desire.

The dominant motifs are trespass, ownership, rootedness, selfhood, and mistaken perception. Syson trespasses physically in the wood and emotionally in Hilda’s life; Pilbeam guards both territory and relationship; Hilda resists being treated as an extension of another person’s imagination. The story’s deepest irony is that Syson, who prides himself on perception, has failed to see Hilda as she is. Its style therefore combines lyrical naturalism with a severe critique of romantic idealisation. The concluding episode, observed covertly through bushes, replaces Syson’s literary fantasy with the physical intimacy of Hilda and Pilbeam. Yet the ending offers no simple victory: Hilda retains distance even from her lover, Pilbeam remains anxious, and Syson leaves wounded but newly aware. The overall tone is elegiac, sensuous, ironic, and emotionally unsparing.

generation.response_text:
I

John Adderley Syson left the train at Wellingborough Halt with a small leather bag, although he had no need of luggage. He was to sleep in town at the King’s Head and return to London next afternoon. The bag, like the silver-headed cane he carried, belonged to the ceremonious version of himself which appeared whenever he went back among people who had known him poor.

The April morning shone with a pale, uncommitted brightness. Beyond the station hedge the country lifted in long green backs, each hill carrying its dark wood like a bearskin garment flung over one shoulder. Rain had fallen before dawn. The road was black at the edges, and in every hoof-mark a little sky trembled.

He stood listening. Somewhere behind the goods shed a chaffinch poured out its hard, crystalline phrase. A cart moved invisibly in the valley. Then, from the wet fields, came the smell of young grass, clay, nettles, and the cold white flowering of blackthorn.

Still the same, he thought.

The thought moved through him almost with physical sweetness. The years in London—his marriage, his reviews and lectures, rooms blue with tobacco smoke, dinners where clever persons glimmered and vanished like fish in an aquarium—dropped away. He was twenty-two again, lean and ardent, walking these roads with books under his arm and Hilda Millership waiting at the farm.

He turned from the high road into a lane whose banks rose above his shoulders. Hazel branches leaned out, their first leaves opening like glad little hands. Beneath them grew dog-mercury, dark and dull, and here and there woodruff made a green star. Primroses watched from the roots, not merely yellow as he remembered them, but cream, faint pink, even one bruised into a pale purple at the heart. The earth had been prodigal while he was away.

Yet he had not been away entirely. For nine years he had written to Hilda: first every week, then every month, then whenever some sudden remembrance obliged him. Books went with the letters—Dante, French verse, a little volume of William Morris, reproductions of Botticelli women who carried their remote, curved mouths through worlds of sorrow. At Christmas he sent silk, scent, once a small Florentine brooch. He had imagined these things entering the farmhouse and making a secret chamber there: an apartment of the mind where he and Hilda continued unchanged.

Marian knew of the letters. He had never hidden them from his wife, because concealment would have made them vulgar. Marian had smiled in her delicate fashion and called Hilda his woodland saint.

“A saint ought to have relics,” Syson had answered.

He had said it brilliantly. He always knew when he had said something brilliantly; the knowledge gave him a little internal bow.

Now, nearing the first spinney, he wondered if Hilda wore the brooch. He saw it at her throat, fastening the plain brown stuff she preferred. She would have grown fuller, perhaps, but not altered. Her nature had been finished early, like the kernel inside a nut: close, pale, complete. She had needed only warmth—his warmth—to ripen.

A pheasant rose almost beneath his feet, beating the air with a furious noise. Syson started and laughed. The bird sailed heavily across the young larches, its copper body burning in the sunlight, and disappeared into the private wood.

A notice was nailed to an oak:

TRESPASSERS WILL BE PROSECUTED.

The path he wanted ran directly beneath it.

He paused, amused by the coarse legal word. Trespass! As though familiarity could become trespass merely because years had intervened. He had walked there before the present owner bought the estate; Hilda had shown him the path. On one June evening they had found white butterflies asleep upon the grasses, innumerable and frail, like petals that had forgotten to fall.

He climbed the bank and entered.

Immediately the world changed. The road, fields, and far farms were extinguished. Pine trunks rose brick-red and purplish from mats of brown needles. In the hollows, bluebells spread in azure shallows, so dense that the eye seemed to wade through colour. Here and there a late daffodil stood among them, a yellow ruffled bird surprised into stillness. Sunlight came down in separate columns, powdering the gnats.

Syson walked softly, almost reverently. His own footfall offended him. This was the eternal country, the preserved country, where youth remained stored beneath leaves. He felt that if he turned sharply enough he might catch sight of his former self—a narrow-shouldered young man in a worn coat—passing between the trees ahead.

Instead he saw another man.

The fellow stood in the path twenty yards away, a gun broken over one arm. He was young, perhaps twenty-five, with a brown, narrow face and eyes of a peculiar grey brightness. His keeper’s coat fitted badly at the shoulders because the shoulders themselves thrust too strongly. Even at rest he seemed balanced for movement, the chest lifted, the legs lightly apart. Syson had an impression not of strength exactly, but of animal tension, life wound tight upon itself.

The keeper waited until Syson approached.

“This path’s private.”

His voice was quiet. That made the challenge more distinct.

“I am aware of the notice,” Syson replied.

“Then you can read.”

Syson glanced at him. “I congratulate us both.”

The keeper’s eyes did not alter.

“You’ll have to go back.”

“I am going to Millership’s farm.”

“Road’s round the other side.”

“I know the road. I also know this path.”

“You’ve no leave to use it.”

Syson felt the old country, which a moment before had opened to receive him, contract with sudden hostility. He smiled.

“My name is Syson. John Adderley Syson.”

He expected recognition, though he could not have said why.

It came. The keeper shifted the gun slightly and looked at him from boots to hat.

“Oh,” he said. “You.”

The monosyllable struck more intimately than any greeting.

“You have the advantage of me.”

“Arthur Pilbeam.”

The name was familiar. Hilda had mentioned a Pilbeam family: labourers at Langley End, people of no account except that one of them bred good lurchers. Syson searched his letters and found, two years back, a reference to “young Arthur, who has taken the keepering.” Nothing more.

“You know Miss Millership, I believe,” Pilbeam said.

“I have known her since she was sixteen.”

“That ain’t what I asked.”

“No?” Syson’s laughter sounded in the wood, thin and brilliant. A blackbird sprang from the bracken at the noise. “Then perhaps you will improve the question.”

Pilbeam’s brown face reddened under the cheekbones.

“You’ve kept sending things.”

“Have I?”

“You know you have. Letters. Books. A little gold pin.”

“Silver-gilt, if the matter requires accuracy.”

“She don’t want ’em.”

“She has not told me so.”

“She wouldn’t.”

“Then I must decline to receive her wishes through a gamekeeper.”

For the first time Pilbeam moved toward him. It was no more than half a pace, yet Syson felt his own body become conspicuously slight, metropolitan, dressed. The young man’s hands were reddish and scratched, one thumb blackened at the nail. They looked capable of taking hold.

“You leave her be,” Pilbeam said. “You’ve got a wife.”

The wood seemed to listen. Far overhead a pigeon beat its wings and settled.

Syson’s smile remained, but it belonged now to his face alone.

“My domestic arrangements can hardly concern you.”

“They concern her.”

“On the contrary. Miss Millership and I have an understanding that existed before you were old enough to carry that gun.”

Pilbeam’s mouth hardened.

“Understanding! You’ve got a fine word for it. You went off. She stayed. You married some town woman. Then you send poetry back, as if words was a bit of string you could tie round her.”

Syson stared at him.

For one instant the young man appeared grotesque—an underkeeper presuming to interpret relations whose refinement he could not conceive. Then something in the phrase about string caused Syson an obscure uneasiness. It had Hilda’s severity in it. Had she spoken so? Had these two discussed him in some low room, at some hour of bodily confidence?

The thought gave him a little sickness.

“You seem well informed,” he said.

“I know what I know.”

“And what, precisely, is your claim?”

The keeper went still. In that stillness Syson recognised the answer before it came.

“She loves me.”

There was no triumph in the statement. Pilbeam spoke almost angrily, as if love were a difficult animal entrusted to him, apt to escape or bite.

Syson looked past him into the bluebells. Their colour had become excessive, unreal, a painted phosphorescence lying over the dead leaves.

“My dear fellow,” he said, “that is a large assertion.”

“You ask her.”

“I intend to.”

Pilbeam hesitated. Jealousy showed nakedly in his face, and because it was naked Syson despised it; because it was powerful he envied it.

“You going there now?”

“Yes.”

“She knows?”

“No.”

The keeper closed the gun with a small, decisive click.

“You’d best take the road.”

Syson stepped aside from the path, as though examining a spray of hyacinth.

“I shall take whichever way pleases me.”

For several seconds neither man moved. Then Pilbeam’s anger passed into something like misery.

“Don’t make trouble for her.”

The appeal, sudden and unwilling, disarmed Syson more than threat had done. He looked again at the young body, the thrusting chest beneath its rough cloth, the anxious grey eyes. This was not a rival fashioned from his own scale of values. It was another order of being.

“I have never made trouble for Hilda,” he said.

Pilbeam gave a short, incredulous breath.

“You don’t know, do you?”

“Know what?”

But the keeper had turned away. He went between the pines without looking back, moving so lightly that the wood seemed to close behind him.

Syson remained among the bluebells. A linnet called from the sunny edge; the sound fell bright and minute into the silence.

He had come home, and already he had been accused of trespass.

II

Millership’s farm stood in a folded valley beyond the wood. Its roofs appeared first, reddish-brown among orchards foamed with blossom; then the long stone wall, a straw stack, and the dark squares of windows. A brook went past the garden, carrying the reflection of marsh-marigolds so that gold floated brokenly over brown water.

Syson stopped at the gate.

Nothing was altered. The iron latch retained its bent neck. A stone trough leaned beneath the yew. Even the elder tree by the dairy had the same split trunk, though one half was dead and diapered with grey fungus. The place endured with an almost insulting fidelity.

He had expected emotion, perhaps tears. Instead he felt watched by his own memory.

A woman crossed the yard carrying a basket of linen. For a moment he thought it was Mrs Millership; then she set down the basket and raised her face.

“You?—Addy!”

Hilda stood with both hands resting on the wicker rim.

She was not as he had pictured her, and yet no single alteration could account for the difference. Her body had become full without heaviness. The sleeves were rolled above her elbows, showing firm arms coloured by sun; her throat rose brown and smooth from an open collar. Her hair, once soft and indefinite, was gathered in a thick crown the colour of beech leaves after rain. The face was broader. Only the eyes remained their old greenish hazel, though even these seemed to look from deeper within herself.

“Hilda,” he said.

She came to him, not running, but with a quickness that shook the light across her face. She held out both hands. He took them and kissed her cheek. Her skin was warm; she smelled faintly of soap, linen, and cows.

“Well!” she said. “You never told us.”

“I wanted to find out whether surprise still existed in England.”

“You look very grand.”

“And you look—”

He paused. The correct phrase failed him.

“Like a farm woman?” she supplied.

“Like yourself.”

She studied him, and he had the uncomfortable sense that her study was more exact than his own. He had put on weight about the eyes; his hair was thinning at the temples. In London these changes composed distinction. Here, under Hilda’s clear gaze, they might signify merely time.

“Come in,” she said. “Mother’s lying down. Her rheumatism’s bad.”

They entered the kitchen. The flagged floor shone from washing. Copper pans gave back small distorted suns; bunches of thyme and lavender hung from the beam; on the deep sill a bowl held scarlet and pink primroses mixed with pale purple ones. Syson recognised the blue bowl. Once Hilda had filled it with cherries while he read aloud from Dante, translating carelessly and stopping whenever she laughed.

He touched the rim.

“You kept it.”

“Why shouldn’t I?”

“Things disappear.”

“Some do.”

She set bread and cheese on the table, then brought cider. There was no flutter in her service. She moved calmly in the room, her skirt brushing her ankles, her bare forearms crossing and recrossing before him. He watched them with a curiosity that seemed almost disloyal to his memories. He had always thought of her hands—her fine fingers holding a page, a flower, a pencil. He had forgotten that the hands belonged to arms, the arms to a living and considerable body.

“You’ve been well?” she asked.

“Industriously well. Marian sends her regards.”

The name entered the kitchen like a person dressed for another climate.

“That was kind.”

“You would like her.”

“Would I?”

“She has great delicacy of perception.”

Hilda cut the bread. “Then perhaps she wouldn’t like me.”

“Why not?”

“I’ve not much delicacy.”

“My dear Hilda, you have the finest instinct of anyone I know.”

She smiled slightly. “That isn’t what you used to say.”

“What did I say?”

“That I must learn to distinguish. Everything was distinctions with you. This love from that love, beauty from prettiness, feeling from sensation. You were forever sorting me.”

He laughed, but his hand tightened on the glass.

“At twenty-two one sorts the universe. Later one is grateful if it remains in the cupboard.”

“You still talk the same.”

“Surely not.”

“The words have grown better clothes.”

He looked up sharply. Her expression was tranquil, almost affectionate. This made the thrust worse.

Outside, hens scratched under the lilac. A bee blundered against the window, fell upon its back, and revolved furiously.

“I met your gamekeeper,” he said.

The knife stopped in Hilda’s hand.

“Arthur?”

“Pilbeam. Yes.”

“Where?”

“In Stainby Wood.”

“You went through the private path?”

“I always went through it.”

“It’s preserved now.”

“So Pilbeam explained with admirable feudal gravity.”

Hilda freed the bee with the corner of a cloth and opened the casement. It flew out into the white blossom.

“What else did he explain?”

“Among other matters, that my correspondence causes distress.”

She turned from the window. A faint colour had appeared beneath her brown skin.

“He had no right.”

“Then it is true?”

“What is true?”

“That my letters trouble him. That you—” He disliked the bluntness of the words and yet had no finer ones. “That you love him.”

Hilda leaned against the sill. The orchard behind her was a confusion of white flowers and blue air, making a brightness around her head which some former Syson would have called a halo. He saw the image arise, saw its falsity, and could not prevent it.

“Yes,” she said.

The simple answer seemed to pass through him without finding a place to lodge.

“You love Arthur Pilbeam.”

“Yes.”

“Well.” He lifted his glass and found it empty. “The sentence acquires no greater plausibility through repetition.”

“Why isn’t it plausible?”

“My dear girl—”

“Don’t call me that.”

The refusal was quiet.

He set down the glass. “Very well. Why him?”

“Because he is himself.”

“Most people suffer from that condition.”

“He doesn’t pretend it’s something else.”

“And I do?”

“You make yourself into words. Then you make everyone else into words too.”

Syson felt anger approach, cool and lucid. “This is unexpectedly metaphysical.”

“It’s plain enough. Arthur knows what I am.”

“And what are you?”

“A woman living here.”

“Nothing more?”

“Everything more. But here.”

He rose and walked to the hearth, where the old black kettle breathed on the hob. Over the mantel hung a coloured print he had given her, Botticelli’s Primavera, faded now to greenish ghosts. The pale women stepped forever through their unreal grove, carrying flowers no season had grown.

“You once desired another life,” he said.

“I desired what you made me see.”

“That is a cruel way of describing awakening.”

“Was I asleep?”

“You had never been given the means to express yourself.”

“And you gave them?”

“I tried.”

She folded the cloth, aligning its corners. “You wanted me to become a person you could admire.”

“I admired you already.”

“No. You admired what you thought was hidden in me. A nun, sometimes. A goddess sometimes. Your Beatrice in muddy boots.” Her mouth curved. “Never me.”

His anger brightened into pain.

“That is unjust. I believed in your possibilities when no one else did. I brought you books. I shared everything I knew.”

“Yes.”

“You encouraged me too. Have you forgotten? When I had the chance to go to London, it was you who said I must. You said I would suffocate here.”

“You would have.”

“You glorified ambition. You told me my work mattered.”

“It did matter.”

“And now my leaving is recast as abandonment.”

“I didn’t say abandonment.”

“Your keeper did.”

“He’s jealous.”

“He is also, I suspect, your spokesman.”

“No.” Her voice hardened. “He speaks badly enough for himself. You needn’t put my words into his mouth, nor his into mine.”

There it was again: the refusal of his arrangement. He felt as though the room, once so receptive to his presence, had acquired edges against which he continually struck.

Hilda came to the table and sat opposite him.

“When you went away,” she said, “I thought I should go too. Not after you. Somewhere else. I read the books and tried to think in the way you’d taught me. Every feeling had to mean another feeling. Every tree was a symbol. If I was lonely, I told myself loneliness was freedom preparing itself.”

“Was that phrase mine?”

“It might have been.”

“It is rather good.”

She looked at him, and unwilling amusement passed between them. For a moment they were restored: conspirators against solemnity, sitting in the old kitchen while rain shut out the world. The moment was so complete that he leaned toward her.

“Hilda—”

But she had already withdrawn.

“Then Father was ill,” she continued. “There was work. Mother couldn’t manage. I stayed. For years I thought staying meant I had failed.”

“Did it not?”

“No.”

The word dropped with the density of a stone.

She looked down at her hands. “One spring I was cutting osiers by the brook. It had flooded, and I stepped too far and went in up to my waist. Arthur pulled me out. We sat under the alders while my clothes dried. He didn’t say I was a river nymph or that the flood was the dark water of the soul. He laughed at me. Then he gave me his coat.”

“How irresistible.”

“Not then. I thought him stupid.”

“And now?”

“Now I know stupidity has many kinds.”

Syson bowed.

“I walked into that.”

“You always walk where there’s a notice.”

He turned to the window. Beyond the orchard, the hill climbed toward Stainby Wood. The pines stood black-green under a sky now deepening into blue. A yellowhammer repeated its little descending song from the hedge, monotonous and exact.

“Do you intend to marry him?”

Hilda was silent.

He looked back. Her face had changed. The assurance remained, but beneath it lay some thought she would not easily offer him.

“No,” she said at last. “Not yet.”

“Does he know?”

“Yes.”

“And he accepts this pastoral uncertainty?”

“He doesn’t like it.”

“Then what is it? Prudence? Your father’s will? A recognition, perhaps, that instinct has social limitations?”

“It is freedom.”

He laughed. The sound was brilliant again, scattering from the copper and glass.

“Freedom! Forgive me. I had not expected to find our old abstractions domesticated so near the pigsties.”

“You see? If I use a word, it is because you once lent it me.”

“I do not claim copyright in the English language.”

“You claim more than that.”

He was suddenly tired. He sat down.

“What do you mean by freedom?”

Hilda answered slowly. “I mean that Arthur comes because he wants me, and I go because I want him. Not because the farm needs a man, or Mother needs someone in the house, or because people say it is time. If I marry him now, everything will close round us—fields, wages, babies, his temper, my duty. Perhaps I shall marry him later. But what we have now is ours.”

The candour of it disturbed him more profoundly than a confession of secret marriage could have done. He saw not innocence deceived by appetite, nor a rustic engagement awaiting respectability, but a woman deliberately holding open a space for desire. This did not accord with his Hilda. His Hilda had possessed a severe inward chastity, a white flame beyond touch.

“You are his mistress,” he said.

The ugliness was intentional.

Hilda flushed, but did not lower her eyes.

“If that is the name you need.”

“And this is fulfilment?”

“Sometimes.”

He got up abruptly. The kitchen seemed too warm, dense with bread, herbs, Hilda’s living body. The Botticelli women on the wall had become absurdly bloodless.

“I should like to see the garden,” he said.

They went outside.

Cloud-shadows travelled over the fields. Along the brook, kingcups burned among reeds, while above them two martins crossed and recrossed the water, stitching the air. Hilda walked without a hat. At the lower gate she put her hand upon the top bar and looked over the meadow.

“This was where you read me the poem about Proserpine,” she said.

“You remember.”

“I remember nearly everything.”

The admission stirred hope against his will.

“Then it was not all illusion.”

“No. It happened.”

“You speak as though that were less than meaning.”

“Things happen first. Meaning comes after and changes them.”

He looked at her profile—the firm chin, the sunlit down upon her cheek, the thick hair pinned above the nape. How had he once seen only a spiritual pallor in this woman? There was nothing pale about her. She was brown, green, warm-coloured, a plant rooted heavily in its own earth.

“You might have come with me,” he said.

“No.”

“You said you wanted to.”

“I wanted to want it.”

“With education, with companionship—”

“I should have died.”

“Not literally, I assume.”

“Perhaps not. But I am like a plant. Move me into a finer pot if you please, give me a conservatory and a Latin name—I grow in this soil.”

“And Pilbeam is the soil?”

“No.” She turned on him. “That is what you always do. If I belong to myself, you must immediately discover whom I belong to instead.”

He had no answer.

From the farmyard came the clang of a bucket, then a man’s voice speaking to the dog. Hilda stiffened almost imperceptibly.

Arthur Pilbeam came through the gate.

He had left his gun and wore no cap. Without the signs of his office he looked younger, but no less taut. His gaze went first to Hilda, then to Syson. A whole conversation of anxiety and reproach passed across his face before he spoke.

“Mr Syson.”

“Mr Pilbeam.”

Hilda remained between them, one hand still on the gate.

“You’ve been to the house, then,” Arthur said.

“As you see.”

“I see.”

“Arthur,” Hilda said, “don’t.”

“I’m not doing anything.”

“No. You’re only filling the field with it.”

Syson smiled. “Miss Millership has been explaining the advantages of unlegalised affection.”

Arthur’s face darkened.

“What’s that to you?”

“Very little, apparently.”

“It ought to be nothing.”

“Arthur!” Hilda’s voice cut sharply.

The young man looked at her. At once his anger became hurt, which he attempted unsuccessfully to conceal.

“He comes back married, walks where he likes, talks how he likes—”

“I have told him,” she said.

“What?”

“Everything that matters.”

Arthur’s eyes searched hers. “And the rest?”

“There is no rest.”

Syson watched them. He had never seen himself look at another human being with Arthur’s naked need, and he felt both superior and impoverished.

“I should go,” he said.

Neither protested.

He bowed to Hilda with a formality that was almost parody. “Thank you for the cider. And the metaphysics.”

“Addy—”

But whatever she might have said was prevented by Arthur’s presence, or by her own unwillingness. Syson waited one second, two. Then he turned up the path beside the brook.

Behind him the silence of the two lovers remained more audible than speech.

III

He did not take the road to town.

At the top of the meadow Syson entered the wood again, though not by the marked path. He moved through young birches and hazel, pushing aside branches wet from the morning rain. The sun had strengthened. Its warmth drew odours from bark, moss, crushed sorrel. Small white flowers of milkwort showed beside the purple lousewort; a bumblebee lowered itself heavily into each bloom like a velvet king.

He told himself he wanted solitude. More exactly, he wanted a conclusion superior to the one Hilda had given him. The conversation at the gate could not be the final form of nine years. There must be some further truth, some refinement in which his pain became intelligible and therefore partly beautiful.

Yet every phrase he composed sounded false.

You wanted me to become a person you could admire.

He struck at a hazel switch with his cane. Its new leaves trembled violently.

Had he done that? Certainly he had urged her to read, to think, to reject the numb fate of a farmer’s daughter. Was influence now a crime? Every love created an image of the beloved; without imagination, desire was merely appetite. He had offered sublimation. She had chosen a gamekeeper’s hut.

He stopped.

Somewhere ahead, Arthur’s voice sounded.

Syson moved cautiously toward it. Through the trees he saw a narrow clearing and, under three pines, a low hut built of boards blackened by weather. A heap of cut bracken lay beside the wall; rabbit wires hung from a nail; above the door a jay’s blue feather had been wedged into a crack.

The keeper stood outside. Hilda faced him.

Syson’s first impulse was to step out and announce himself. But Arthur spoke, and the misery in his tone held Syson motionless.

“You’ll let him write again.”

“I can’t stop a letter coming.”

“You can burn it.”

“I may.”

“May!”

“Don’t begin.”

“You had him there, eating with you.”

“He arrived.”

“You looked glad.”

“I was glad.”

Arthur turned away and kicked at a piece of bark.

Behind a screen of young spruce, Syson felt humiliation rise like heat into his face. He ought not to listen. He knew this with perfect clarity. Yet to leave would be to surrender the only unguarded truth he might ever receive. He remained.

Hilda went nearer to Arthur, but did not touch him.

“I was glad because he belonged to my life once.”

“Once?”

“Yes.”

“He don’t think it’s once. The way he looks at you—like he’s got some secret claim.”

“That is his trouble.”

“Yours too, maybe.”

“No.”

Arthur gave a harsh little laugh. “You use his words.”

“I use any words I please.”

“You talk about freedom and self and all that. You never talked so before his books.”

“I never talked much at all before his books. Do you want me dumb?”

“I want you mine.”

The sentence seemed to frighten him after he had spoken it. His shoulders lifted, and the hands at his sides closed.

Hilda looked at him steadily.

“I am not yours.”

Arthur’s face went grey beneath the brown.

Syson experienced a quick, contemptible pleasure. Here, then, was the limitation of the young man’s confidence. Hilda refused everyone. Her autonomy was merely a polished name for coldness.

Then she raised both hands and took Arthur’s face between them.

“I am not yours,” she repeated, “but I love you.”

He seized her wrists, not roughly, but as if the words had struck him off balance.

“Then marry me.”

“Not now.”

“Why not? You come here. You stay with me. Everyone’ll know sooner or later.”

“Let them.”

“It’s easy for you to say.”

“No, it isn’t.”

“My mother says—”

“I am not marrying your mother.”

“She says you think yourself above us.”

Hilda’s mouth tightened. “And do you?”

“No.”

“You do when he comes. You look at his coat and hear his talk, and then you think I must be comparing you.”

“Aren’t you?”

“Yes,” she said.

Arthur released her wrists.

The cruelty of the answer made even Syson draw breath. But Hilda followed Arthur as he turned toward the hut.

“I compare everyone,” she said. “You compare too. He knows poems. You know where the vixen crosses after rain. He can make a room listen. You can wait three hours without moving. He sees meanings in everything. You see what is there.”

“And which do you want?”

“You.”

Arthur looked at her over his shoulder.

“All of me?”

“All that you are. Not what you might become if I worked at you.”

The echo of her accusation against Syson was unmistakable. He felt it enter him with a slow, surgical precision.

Arthur sat on the step of the hut. Hilda remained standing. For some moments there was no sound but the small, liquid ticking of a wren among the roots.

“He’s passed out, then?” Arthur asked.

“Yes.”

“Clean out?”

“Clean out of my life.”

Syson closed his eyes.

He had thought pain might come as violence, a tearing or collapse. Instead the statement produced an enormous stillness. In that stillness he saw his letters arriving year after year, their envelopes placed on the kitchen mantel; the books opened, perhaps read, perhaps not; the Florentine brooch lying in a drawer among buttons. He had inhabited no secret chamber. He had been paper entering a house.

Arthur said, “You won’t write back?”

“No.”

“Nor meet him?”

“He may come. It makes no difference.”

“What if he says he loves you?”

“He doesn’t.”

“He does.”

“No. He loves the light he used to see round me. He made it himself.”

The precision was intolerable. Syson wanted to step forward and deny her, to explain the serious and incorruptible quality of what he had felt. Yet the young spruce pressed softly against his sleeve, and he remained hidden like a thief.

Arthur looked toward the trees. Syson froze. But the keeper saw nothing.

“What was he to you?” Arthur asked.

Hilda sat beside him.

“He opened a window,” she said. “Before Addy, I thought the farm was the whole world because it was all I knew. Then he showed me there were cities, pictures, languages, people who lived by the mind. For a while I thought the window was a door, and that I must go through.”

“Why didn’t you?”

“I looked long enough.”

“And shut it?”

“No. I know the world is there. That is different from having to leave this one.”

Arthur picked up her hand and examined the palm, tracing a line in it with his blackened thumb.

“You’ll tire of me.”

“Perhaps.”

“You say things like that to hurt.”

“I say them because promises can be another kind of lie.”

“I could promise.”

“I know.”

“I’d never look at another woman.”

“You would.”

“I wouldn’t!”

Hilda smiled, not mockingly. “You’re alive, Arthur.”

“What’s that mean?”

“It means I don’t want your goodness if it has to strangle you.”

He stared at her in bewilderment. Syson almost smiled. There were his ideas again, altered by her, brought down from their philosophical heights and made to walk barefoot in the dirt. He had taught her freedom as a noble abstraction; she used it to refuse marriage while sitting beside her lover’s bed.

For the hut had a bed. Through the open doorway Syson could see the dim interior: a rough table, a chair, a lamp, the corner of a narrow mattress covered by a brown blanket. On a shelf stood one of the books he had sent Hilda, its green spine unmistakable. Morris’s poems.

The discovery shocked him more than the bed.

The book had crossed over. His gift, intended as a bridge between Hilda and himself, stood in the hidden room she shared with Arthur. It belonged to their intimacy now. Perhaps she had read aloud there. Perhaps the keeper had listened, his head on her lap, understanding little and possessing everything.

Hilda rose.

“I must go back.”

Arthur caught her hand. “Stay a bit.”

“Mother will wake.”

“Five minutes.”

“You said that yesterday.”

“Stay.”

His plea was boyish, but his body as he stood before her was not. He drew her close. At first she held herself separate, head lifted, the crown of her hair bright in the light beyond the pines. Then something in her gave way—not submission, Syson saw, but consent. Her arms went round Arthur’s neck.

The young man bent his face into the warm hollow below her ear. Hilda closed her eyes. Her expression lost its thoughtfulness, its defensive intelligence. It became deep, grave, almost blind. She pressed him against her with the strength of her whole body.

Syson could not look away.

No painted Primavera, no Beatrice in a crimson robe, no white nun behind a grille could survive that embrace. Hilda was not translated by it into spirit. She was brought more densely into herself: her brown arms, her throat, her weight upon the earth. Arthur’s hand spread across her back. They stood rooted together, two forms of the same urgent life, yet even now not merged. Syson saw Hilda’s fingers loosen in the keeper’s hair, then close again by choice.

She whispered something.

Arthur lifted his head. “What?”

“I said, don’t be afraid of him.”

“I’m not.”

“You are.”

“He’s clever.”

“So are foxes.”

“He’s got the world.”

“No one has the world.”

“You think he’s finer than me.”

“In some ways.”

Arthur flinched.

“In others,” she continued, “he is less real than that feather.”

She touched the blue jay’s feather above the hut door.

Syson felt the judgment land upon him with curious finality. Less real than a feather: he who had interpreted, distinguished, illuminated. He had made the world into language so completely that language now stood between him and existence like glass.

Arthur kissed her. This time there was no hesitation. Hilda received the kiss, then ended it, placing both palms upon his chest.

“I am going.”

“Tomorrow?”

“If I can.”

“Tonight?”

“No.”

He looked toward the bed.

She laughed softly. “Greedy.”

“You like me greedy.”

“Sometimes.”

“Marry me at midsummer.”

“We’ll see.”

“That means no.”

“It means the year hasn’t reached May.”

She passed her hand down his cheek, and the tenderness of the gesture was more painful to Syson than their kiss.

Then Hilda went away between the trees.

She came so near his hiding place that he could see a loose strand of hair against her throat. If she had turned her head, she must have discovered him. But she walked on, looking ahead. Whether some instinct told her he was there, he never knew.

Arthur remained outside the hut. His whole body listened after her. At last he took the jay’s feather from the crack and turned it between finger and thumb. Then he went inside and shut the door.

Syson waited.

The wood resumed itself by degrees. A beetle moved over the wet bark beside his hand, black with a violet lustre. Midges revolved in a beam of sunshine. From the valley came the faint calling of cattle, and farther off the church clock struck four, each note entering the trees round and slow.

Still the same. Unaltered.

But the phrase no longer comforted him. The wood had not preserved his youth; it had merely continued without it. Bluebells spread where they had always spread, and each spring was wholly itself, not a repetition designed for his return. He had mistaken recurrence for fidelity.

He emerged from the spruces and stood before the hut.

He could knock. He imagined Arthur opening the door and finding him there, pale, smiling, terrible in his knowledge. There might be a scene: accusation, irony, perhaps even a blow. Such drama would at least restore him to the centre.

He did not knock.

On the ground lay a page torn from some old sporting paper. Rain had blurred the print until horses, advertisements, and results flowed together in grey streams. Syson prodded it with his cane, then turned away.

The shortest route to Wellingborough descended by the quarry and crossed the high fields. He took it slowly.

Toward evening the sky cleared to an immaculate blue. Clouds withdrawn to the east stood in rose-coloured towers. The wet hedges shone; hawthorn buds showed green-white among black twigs; on the ploughed land rooks walked with purple shoulders, solemn as minor priests. Every ditch, tree, bird, and stone appeared distinct, marvellous, for ever new.

The beauty oppressed him.

He had always believed that perception redeemed pain. To see clearly was to transform suffering into form; to name a colour, a movement, a quality of light was already to rise above it. But now the world’s loveliness repeated itself without relief. Blue after blue, gold after gold, blossom after blossom—the inexhaustible radiance became a monotone hell.

At the crest of the hill he looked back.

Millership’s farm lay small in the valley, smoke ascending straight from one chimney. The brook caught the sunset in three red fragments. Stainby Wood had become a single dark mass, concealing the hut, Arthur, Hilda, all that bodily and local life from which Syson felt himself expelled.

Yet expelled was not the true word. One could only be expelled from a place one had entered. He had never entered Hilda’s life. He had stood outside it, describing the windows.

The recognition wounded his vanity first. He saw the letters he had written, the subtle confidences, the quotations chosen with exquisite relevance. How generous, how faithful he had considered himself! In truth he had maintained Hilda as one keeps a lamp burning before an image: not for the image’s sake, but to illuminate one’s own devotion.

Then, beneath vanity, another pain opened—quieter, almost tender.

He had loved her. Not as she was; he could not claim that now. But something in him had reached toward something in her, and if the reaching had failed, it had not been wholly false. Youth itself had spoken through them, lavish and mistaken. Hilda had taken from him a window. He had taken from her a figure of permanence. Neither gift had remained what the giver intended.

He thought of Marian in London, arranging flowers on the dining table with her fine, undecided hands. Had he seen her more clearly? Or had he made of her another necessary form—wife, companion, intelligence—while some actual woman lived behind the names?

The question frightened him.

At the station road darkness had begun to collect beneath the elms. A thrush sang from the upper branches, repeating its phrases with obstinate sweetness. Near the ditch, the first stitchwort flowers shone white. Syson bent and picked one, then immediately regretted it. Severed, it looked meagre in his hand.

He let it fall.

A cart overtook him. The driver, an old man folded into a green coat, raised his whip.

“Goin’ town way, sir?”

“Yes.”

“Get up, then. Road’s none too dry.”

Syson climbed beside him. The cart smelled of sacks, horse, and turnips. Its wheels entered every rut with a jolt that defeated thought. The old man spoke of rain, lambing, the price of feed. Syson answered when required.

At the edge of town, lamps appeared one by one in the dusk. Windows glowed behind curtains. A woman called a child indoors. Somewhere a piano stumbled through a hymn.

“You lodging at the King’s Head?” the driver asked.

“For tonight.”

“London tomorrow?”

“Yes.”

“Ah. London.” The old man considered the word without admiration. “Couldn’t abide it myself.”

“No,” Syson said. “Perhaps one must be transplanted young.”

The driver glanced at him, found nothing practical in the remark, and clicked to the horse.

At the inn Syson went up to his room. It was narrow and smelled of coal dust and lavender furniture polish. He set his bag upon the bed, removed his gloves, and stood before the spotted mirror.

The face within it looked older than the one that had left the train that morning. He knew this was sentiment; faces did not age in a day. Nevertheless, some expression had been stripped from him. The eyes appeared less protected.

On the table lay writing paper stamped with the inn’s crest. He sat down.

Dear Hilda,

He stopped.

He might write nobly: forgive the intrusion; be happy; our friendship has passed into another phase. He could quote something—Dante’s final vision, perhaps, or the line from the French poem about love surviving its own object. He could fashion the day into a last gift, beautifully phrased and therefore still partly his.

He tore the sheet across.

On another he wrote:

Dear Marian,  
I shall return by the noon train tomorrow.

After a pause he added:

I have much to tell you, though I do not yet know what it is.

That sentence seemed dangerously close to effect. He considered striking it out, but let it remain.

He opened the window. The town roofs descended toward the unseen country. Above them the night was dark blue, and one star burned with steady, impersonal brightness.

Somewhere beyond the hills Hilda would be moving through the farmhouse, setting the supper, tending her mother, perhaps thinking of Arthur, perhaps not thinking of either man. The freedom she claimed did not need Syson’s understanding. This was the final injury and the first truth.

He stood a long while at the window.

Then he folded Marian’s letter, extinguished the lamp, and allowed the countryside to disappear into its own darkness.

# The Museum of Unfinished Things

Every morning at nine, Mara Venn unlocked the Museum of Unfinished Things.

She opened the brass gates, wound the clock above the entrance, and crossed the marble hall while her footsteps multiplied in the glass display cases. Sunlight came through the high windows in pale ladders, illuminating dust, chipped statues, half-painted canvases, and machines whose inventors had abandoned them before discovering whether they worked.

The museum stood at the edge of Bellweather, where the city ended and the salt marshes began. It had no gift shop, no café, and few visitors. Children found it disappointing. Adults found it uncomfortable.

Mara preferred it that way.

Her first task was always to inspect the exhibits.

In the Hall of Letters rested hundreds of envelopes that had never been sent. Some lacked stamps. Some lacked addresses. One contained nothing but the words, “I was wrong,” written in green ink.

In the Gallery of Inventions, a mechanical bird waited with one brass wing attached and the other represented only by a charcoal sketch. Nearby stood an umbrella designed to collect rainwater and turn it into music. Its pipes had never been tuned.

The western wing held larger things: an unfinished bridge, assembled indoors and pointing nowhere; a staircase of seven steps, intended for a house that had never been built; and the skeleton of a wooden ship whose absent hull seemed to rise around it whenever fog pressed against the windows.

Mara checked each label, polished each case, and noted every crack or change in color. She had worked at the museum for eleven years, though she was only thirty-two. The previous curator, Mr. Vale, had trained her since childhood.

“Completed things tell you what they are,” he had once said. “Unfinished things ask who they might have been.”

At the time, Mara had thought this very wise.

Now she suspected it was merely sad.

At ten minutes past nine, the bell over the entrance rang.

Mara looked up from a case containing a violin without strings.

A boy stood inside the door.

He was perhaps twelve, narrow-shouldered and rain-soaked, though the sky outside was clear. Water dripped from his dark hair onto his coat. He carried a small wooden box beneath one arm.

“We’re not open to donations without an appointment,” Mara said.

“I don’t have an appointment.”

“Then you’ll need to make one.”

“With you?”

“Yes.”

“For now?”

“That is not how appointments work.”

The boy considered this. “What if it’s important?”

“Everything donated here is important to someone.”

“This is important to everyone.”

Mara sighed. She had already learned that solemn children were often more exhausting than noisy ones.

“What is it?”

The boy placed the box on the admissions desk. It was made of black wood, bound by a silver latch. A pattern had been carved into the lid: a circle interrupted just before its ends touched.

Mara’s irritation vanished.

“My mother left it for me.”

“Who is your mother?”

“Lena Or.”

Mara stepped back.

Mara had been twenty then. She remembered waiting beside the museum telephone until dawn, convinced it would ring.

For Eli, when the museum clock begins to lose time.

Mara understood.

The museum had been founded to preserve what people abandoned. Yet preservation had become refusal—the refusal to let lost futures become lost.

She thought of eleven years spent dusting unsent letters and broken machines. She had told herself she was guarding possibility. In truth, she had been waiting. For Mr. Vale. For Lena. For her old life to resume.

It never would.

She placed her palm against the door.

“What are you doing?” Lena asked.

“My job.”

Mara closed her eyes.

She thought of the green-ink letter in the Hall of Letters.

It would never be sent.

The mechanical bird would never fly.

The bridge would never reach another shore.

Her father would remain dead. Her childhood was over. The person she might have married was a stranger. The music she might have played had never been written.

Mr. Vale would not come home.

Lena could not recover the years she had lost with her son.

“These things are finished,” Mara said.

The visions beyond the door trembled.

“No,” whispered a thousand voices.

Mara pushed.

The door moved an inch.

“They are unfinished,” Lena said, understanding, “and that is how they ended.”

She placed her hand beside Mara’s.

Eli joined them.

Mr. Vale released the knob at last and leaned his weight against the wood.

Together, they pushed.

The imagined stars went dark one by one. Unbuilt cities folded into dust. Unlived lives faded without ceremony. The Lower Museum roared around them, not in anger but in grief.

The door closed.

The latch clicked.

For a moment, nothing happened.

Then the basement became the basement again.

There were stone walls, a low ceiling, and one green door. Mr. Vale lay on the floor. His breathing was shallow.

Mara knelt beside him.

“Did we finish it?” she asked.

He looked at the closed door.

“Yes.”

“Can you come home now?”

“My dear girl,” he murmured, “I was always coming home. It only took longer than expected.”

He died before they carried him upstairs.

The museum reopened six months later.

Repairs took time. The west wing returned without its gray sea, though salt remained in the cracks between the floorboards. The unfinished ship stood in its old place, stubborn and dry.

Mara made changes.

She removed the word *preserved* from the museum’s official purpose and replaced it with *remembered*. She installed new labels describing not only what each object might have become, but why it had been abandoned.

Some stories were tragic. Others were ordinary. The rainwater umbrella had been left incomplete because its inventor became a baker and discovered she preferred making bread.

The green-ink letter remained unsent because its writer apologized in person.

The mechanical bird’s creator had simply grown tired of brass.

Visitors began to return.

Lena came often, though she never again worked as a curator. She and Eli were learning to know one another. It was not easy. Some days they left the museum laughing; other days, separately.

Mara did not interfere.

Above the admissions desk hung a portrait of Mr. Vale, painted from memory. It was unfinished. The artist had omitted his hands.

One rainy afternoon, Eli found Mara beneath it, repairing the museum clock.

“It’s losing time again,” he said.

“No. It stopped.”

“Is that bad?”

Mara glanced toward the western wing.

Nothing vanished. No sea appeared. The building remained solid around them, full of incomplete objects that were no longer waiting to become something else.

She climbed down from the ladder.

“No,” she said. “Clocks stop.”

Eli looked doubtful. “Shouldn’t you fix it?”

“Perhaps tomorrow.”

Together they stood beneath the silent clock as visitors moved through the halls. A child laughed beside the stringless violin. Someone read the unsent letters. Rain tapped against the windows, each drop sounding like a tiny knock from the other side of a door.

Mara listened until the sound became only rain.

Then she turned off the lights, closed the museum, and went home.
